opening.headline: Understand what each part of the OpenAI Agents SDK does and how it fits together in one map.
body: The reason it is difficult to know where to start when the agent app behaves strangely is not because there are many parts, but because the tasks of each part cannot be distinguished. Agent definitions, execution loops, tool linking, conversation memory, and observation devices take on different problems.

In this class, we will look at the Agents, Runners, Tools, MCP, Sessions, and Tracing of the OpenAI Agents SDK in turn, followed by the configuration and error handling of the hosted Agents API. At the end, we follow the sequence of events through a single execution of a handoff, and organize where to look if something goes wrong.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the roles of agents, tools, executors, sessions, and tracing
Agents API settings and error handling structures can be distinguished.
Handoff and agent-as-tool can be distinguished by where control resides.

screens.title: I made an agent and I don't know what happened
screens.lead: First, read what's going on with the team that created the customer support app. I read this while thinking about why it is difficult to determine which part has the problem.

visual.alt: A scene demonstrating two issues: an app showing the transition from classifier agent to refund agent, and an unknown issue.

paragraphs: A team created a customer support app. When a refund request comes in, the classification agent hands over the task to a refund specialist agent. At first it seemed to work fine.

However, the user reported that “an incorrect answer was received.” There was no way to know which agent called which tool. Some tool calls failed and the app silently froze, not knowing if I should retry.

Agent definitions, execution loops, tool connections, conversation memories, and observation devices are all played out separately, so it's hard to know where to start. When there seem to be a lot of parts provided by the SDK, the first thing you need is to organize the tasks of each part into a single map.
This class asks one question. What do each of these parts do and how do they fit together? Find the answer by following the configuration of the OpenAI Agents SDK and Agents API.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: When an incorrect answer is given, what should be recorded to determine whether “the definition is wrong, the loop is wrong, the tool is wrong, or the memory is wrong?”

screens.outro: Let me first think about whether you have had a similar experience.

screens.title: Think of similar scenes
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think in your head first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever had a multi-step automation where you had to spend time trying to figure out which step went wrong?
items.answer: If the inputs and outputs of each step are not recorded, you will have to guess the cause by looking only at the final result. Because agent execution involves model invocation, tool invocation, and handover, an observatory device that records each step is particularly important.

items.prompt: Have you ever had trouble continuing the same conversation but not being able to remember the previous content?
items.answer: The model only knows what it receives as input for each call. To continue a previous conversation, you need a memory device to store the conversation record somewhere and then restore it. The part that takes on this role is the session.

items.prompt: Have you ever had an external system call fail occasionally and need a retry rule?
items.answer: Transient connection errors and errors in which the request itself is invalid are handled differently. The former requires a limited number of retries, and the latter requires correcting the input. You need to know the structure of reading errors by type.

items.prompt: What kind of map will this class draw?
items.answer: This lesson provides a one-page map of how each part of the OpenAI Agents SDK takes on these problems. Agent definitions, Runners, tools, sessions, tracing, and configuration and error handling of the Agents API.

screens.outro: First, let's look at the code to define an agent.

screens.title: Agent Definition: Instructions, Tools and Handovers
screens.lead: Please read the code alternately with the explanation on the right. This is the minimum configuration where a sorting agent hands over work to a refund agent.

data.code:
from agents import Agent, Runner, function_tool

@function_tool
def lookup_refund(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Check whether a refund is possible using the order number."""
    return "Refundable: within 14 days of purchase"

refund_agent = Agent(
    name="Refund agent",
    instructions="Handle refund inquiries. Answer only the facts confirmed with the inquiry tool.",
    tools=[lookup_refund],
)

triage_agent = Agent(
    name="Triage agent",
    instructions="Inquiries are sorted and refund inquiries are forwarded to the refund agent.",
    handoffs=[refund_agent],
)

result = Runner.run_sync(
    triage_agent, "I would like to refund order 1234.", max_turns=10
)
print(result.final_output)

notes.note: `@function_tool` turns Python functions into tools. A schema is automatically generated from function signatures and verified with Pydantic. The docstring is used specifically because it provides a description for the model to determine when to use the tool.

The agent is an LLM with a name, instructions, and tools. A name and instructions alone define a minimal agent. If the instructions are vague, you may be confused about when to call the tool and when not to call it.

`handoffs` is a device that passes work to another agent. It looks like a tool to the model, and handoffs to the refund agent appear as tool calls starting with `transfer_to_`. If the description of the handover target is unclear, the wrong agent will be selected.
`Runner.run_sync` takes the startup agent and input and loops. `max_turns` is the iteration limit to prevent runaway, and `result.final_output` contains the final output.

screens.outro: Now that we have the definitions, let's look at the Runner that actually executes these definitions.

screens.title: Runner: The side that runs the agent loop
screens.lead: Select the right arrow and follow the Runner step-by-step through the agent loop.

visual.alt: Illustration of a cycle where the Runner repeats the LLM call, handoff, and tool call.
labels: Call LLM with your current agent

steps.title: Three ways to run
steps.body: Runner has three running methods: `run()` is asynchronous, `run_sync()` is synchronous, and `run_streamed()` receives events as streaming. Just choose a method that fits the structure of the app.

steps.title: Start Agent and Input
steps.body: If you give it a start agent and input, it will loop. The input can be a string, a list of items in Responses format, or `RunState`, which continues execution where it stopped.

steps.title: Call LLM
steps.body: The loop starts by calling LLM as the current agent. If the output is final, the loop ends and the result is returned.

steps.title: Handles handoffs
steps.body: When the LLM requests a handoff, it swaps its input with the current agent and loops again. This is the moment when a sorting agent turns into a refund agent.

steps.title: Handles tool calls
steps.body: When the tool call comes up, it runs the tool, appends the results to the input, and loops again. This iteration continues until the final output is produced.

steps.title: repetition limit
steps.body: If `max_turns` is exceeded, a `MaxTurnsExceeded` exception occurs. This limit is a surge prevention device and can be turned off with `None`, but turning it off will remove any device to prevent repetition. From the result object, `final_output` and the state to be continued are taken out.

screens.outro: Next, let's look at the tools used by the agent and MCP connections.

screens.title: Connect your tools to your MCP
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn about the types of tools, how to connect to the MCP server, and the principles to follow.

tabs.label: What is a tool?
tabs.body: A tool is a means by which an agent retrieves data, executes code, calls an external API, or uses a computer. An agent's capabilities are limited to the extent of its defined tools. Without the tool, the agent can only say what the model already knows. When adding a new tool, you need to think about what capabilities and risks it brings to your agents.

tabs.label: Category of tools
tabs.body: There is a hosting tool that runs on OpenAI servers. These include web browsing, file browsing, code interpreter, hosting MCP, and image creation. There are also local execution tools running around in my environment, function tools that turn Python functions into tools, agent-as-tools (a way of calling another agent like a tool, compare it to Handoff in the next screen), and Codex tools. The function tool automatically generates schemas and validates them with Pydantic. Which category you choose determines where your code runs and where your data goes.

tabs.label: MCP connection method
tabs.body: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that connects AI apps to external tools and data. The app becomes the client, and the server exposes external functionality, and the server provides tools, resources, and prompts. There are several ways this SDK connects to an MCP server. There is a hosting MCP that calls a public server instead of a model, and the methods that my app connects to directly include Streamable HTTP, SSE, and stdio. Streamable HTTP and SSE are methods of connecting to a remote server via HTTP, and SSE is a method of sending events through an open HTTP connection from the server. stdio is a method in which an app runs the server as a subprocess and communicates with standard input and output. The choice depends on where the server runs and who is brokering the call. The local process is code that runs with the same permissions as your app, and the remote server is across the network, so the trust boundary is different.

tabs.label: safety principles
tabs.body: The MCP server exposes data in the model context and operates with the credentials I gave it. So you should only connect to trusted servers, use credentials with minimal privileges, and require approval for sensitive operations. Place the token in an authentication field or header rather than in the URL. These rules are there for a reason. Tool results and tool information provided by the server become input to the model, and if text that looks like instructions is mixed in, the model can follow. This is called prompt injection, and when it is hidden in external content such as a web page or file, it is called indirect injection. Also, the greater the functions and authority given to the agent, the greater the damage caused by injection or misjudgment of the model. OWASP organizes this into excessive agency and divides the cause into unnecessary functions, authority, and autonomy. Therefore, the basis for the above rule is to connect only the necessary tools, grant minimum privileges, and require human approval for operations that are difficult to reverse. The MCP specification also advises not to trust tool annotations from untrusted servers, and to have a human rejection step in tool calls.

screens.outro: Next, we will compare two ways to delegate work to other agents.

screens.title: Handoff and Agent-as-Tool: Where is the Control?
screens.lead: Alternate between the “Handoff” and “Agent-as-Tool” buttons to compare where the control lies. Both methods delegate the work to different agents, but the conversation takes place differently.

states.label: handoff
states.body: A handoff is a way to transfer a conversation to another agent. It looks like a tool to the model, and the handoff to the refund agent defaults to a call to the tool named `transfer_to_refund_agent`. When a call occurs, the receiving agent takes over the conversation and can essentially view the previous history. What to show on the receiving end can be narrowed down with input filters. Since control of the conversation is transferred from the classification agent to the refund agent, it is suitable for a structure in which the person the user is talking to is then replaced by an expert. For example, if a classification agent passes a refund inquiry to a refund agent, the refund agent will handle the rest. Judgment question is one thing. Even after this, should the entity that communicates with users change?

states.label: agent-as-tool
states.body: Agent-as-tool is a way to call another agent like a tool. Created with `Agent.as_tool()`, the calling agent retains control and creates the final answer himself. The inner agent is executed by the tool call, and its final output is returned to the calling agent as the tool result. The caller then refines the results and answers the user. The inner execution does not inherit its parent's state unless it also passes the same session. It is suitable for a structure in which one agent collects the results of multiple experts and organizes them into one answer. For example, a comprehensive agent combines the results of an order inquiry expert and a policy expert to provide an answer. The judgment questions are the same. Should the owner of the conversation be the same agent until the end?

screens.outro: Next, we will look at tracing, which records the sessions and flows that follow conversations.

screens.title: Sessions and Tracing
screens.lead: You can select and expand each item to see how the conversation memory and observation devices work.

items.title: Session: Permanent memory that connects conversation records
items.body: A session is a persistent memory that automatically maintains a conversation history across multiple runs. The session is responsible for re-entering the previous content when the user continues the same conversation. Your memory strategy is determined along with how you use Runner. If there is no session, each call starts like a new conversation.

items.title: Tracing: Visualize and debug flows
items.body: Tracing is built into the SDK, allowing you to visualize, debug, and evaluate agent flows. This is the part that directly answers the problem of the first scene, which is that we don't know what happened. When you open a trace, you can see at a glance which steps took a long time and which tools failed.

items.title: traces and spans
items.body: A trace represents an entire workflow and has `workflow_name`, `trace_id`, and `group_id`, which group traces from the same conversation. A span is an individual task with a start and end time. Agent execution, LLM creation, function tool calls, guardrails, and handoffs are each recorded as spans.

items.title: Default behavior and limitations
items.body: By default, the entire `Runner.run` family of calls is wrapped in one trace. You can also turn it off on a per run basis. However, tracing cannot be used in organizations with a zero data retention policy.

items.title: Relationship with guardrails
items.body: Guardrails run input and output verification and safety checks in parallel with agent execution, failing quickly if they do not pass. The record of guardrail work is also recorded as a span.

screens.outro: Now let's look at the configuration and error handling of the hosted Agents API.

screens.title: Configuration and errors of Agents API
screens.lead: Read the table to see where errors occur in the Agents API and where to read them.

data.caption: Where the Agents API fails and where to check
rows: `error` object of HTTP status and response
It determines whether the request itself is incorrect or whether it is an authentication or authorization issue.
Check the turn after the `agent.session.turn.failed` event and check `status` and `error`
Failures after a task has started are treated separately from request errors.
Check the session after the `agent.session.failed` event and check `status` and `error`
This is the case when the entire session fails.
When using an environment, read the sandbox side failure.
data.notes: The Agents API runs the hosting instance where OpenAI runs the harness, which loops through models and tools and maintains sessions. My app sends a task and receives a result. The environment is where commands and codes are executed and files are handled. If not needed, set the type to none, and if necessary, add a hosting sandbox. Agent configuration consists of models, instructions, tools, inferences, and output formats, which can be given directly to the session or saved for reuse. Errors are structured so that in application logic we write `error.code`, in user description we write `error.message`, and in request validation errors we write `error.param` which field to fix. Temporary errors such as rate limit, overload, connection, and timeout are retried a limited number of times.

screens.outro: Now that we've looked at all the parts, let's follow the sequence of events in an actual run with commentary.

screens.title: Explanation 1: Sequence of events in one run where handoffs occur
screens.lead: The instructor will explain the order in which refund requests for the first scene will be processed in one run. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: 1. Start execution
steps.body: Give classification agent and user input to `Runner.run`. This entire call is wrapped in one trace. From this point on, all steps begin to be recorded as spans. Spans have start and end times, so you can also see how long each step takes.

steps.title: 2. Request a handoff
steps.body: I called LLM as the sorting agent and they requested a handoff to the refund agent. Handoffs appear like tools to the model, so they appear as tool calls starting with `transfer_to_`.

steps.title: 3. Replace the agent
steps.body: The Runner replaces the current agent with the refund agent and starts the loop again. The handoff itself also remains a span. Later, we use this span to check who passed it to whom. At this time, the input is also changed to determine the conversation that the refund agent will take over.

steps.title: 4. Call the tool
steps.body: The refund agent calls the refund lookup function tool. The results of the tool execution are appended to the input and the loop loops again. Tool calls are also recorded as function tool spans and their input values ​​are left with them. If the tool fails, the failure information is appended to the input so the model can determine its next action.

steps.title: 5. Return the final answer
steps.body: When the final answer is found, the loop ends and `final_output` is returned. If you have a session, this conversation history will be saved and carried over to your next call. In this one run, there are at least three model calls, all spanning within the same trace.

screens.outro: Next, I'll explain where to look when a problem arises.

screens.title: Commentary 2: Where do you look when a problem arises?
screens.lead: When you select each symptom, the places to check first will appear. Substitute the reports from the first scene one by one.

items.answer: View the handoff span of the trace. It is revealed in chronological order who handed it over to whom and in what order. You can also get a clue here whether the description of the transfer target was unclear.

items.prompt: Symptom 2: A tool was called with incorrect values.
items.answer: You can view the function tools' span and tool schema. The span records what input the model used to invoke a tool. If the schema or description is ambiguous, the model may incorrectly populate values. Since the input values differ each time a tool is called, you must directly read the values recorded in the span.

Look at the `max_turns` setting and the `MaxTurnsExceeded` exception. Loop iteration limits serve as a safeguard against infinite loops. Verify whether the same tool is being repeatedly invoked by tracing calls. When the limit is disabled, alternative termination conditions are required.

items.prompt: Symptom 4: Turn failed in Agents API.
items.answer: `turn.failed` queries the turn after an event and reads `status` and `error`. The reading location differs depending on whether the failure occurs at the requested, turn, session, or environment level.

items.prompt: Symptom 5: intermittent errors related to connection or overload occur.
items.answer: Treats this using limited retry attempts. The criteria are temporary failures and errors pertaining to the request itself. Request validation errors yield the same result upon retry, so the field indicated by `error.param` is modified.

screens.outro: Finally, we will compare the division of responsibilities between the SDK and the Agents API.

screens.title: Commentary 3: SDK and Agents API, what am I responsible for?
screens.lead: Alternate between the "Agents SDK" and "Agents API" buttons to compare how the same component is managed in each approach. Note that the concept of the component is the same in both methods.

states.label: Agents SDK
states.body: Runner runs loops and handoffs within my app. I control deployment, storage, approval, and runtime integration. Perfect when you need more control. Instead, the burden of distributing and operating the app is also my responsibility. If you want to own the loop yourself or handle tool dispatching and state handling yourself, you also have the option of writing the Responses API directly. For example, if you need to connect the approval process to an in-house system or add it to an existing deployment pipeline, an SDK is the way to go. The SDK is installed and used as a Python package, and uses the Responses API as a base, with a runtime that manages turns, tool execution, guardrails, handoffs, and sessions on top of it.

states.label: Agents API
states.body: Harness is operated by OpenAI. My app sends tasks, receives events, processes function tools, and manages environment lifetimes when necessary. The environment is optional. If your app only performs question-answering or external service calls, leave it as `none`; if scripts or files are needed, attach a hosting environment. This is appropriate when you want to reduce operational overhead. Regardless of the approach, the component concept remains the same, differing only in configuration location. The four questions—agent, tool, session, observation—are verified in the same order across both approaches. By predefining a stored agent, you can reuse the same configuration across multiple sessions.

screens.outro: Lastly, I will summarize the order of problem solving.

screens.title: Checking sequence when the agent answers strangely
screens.lead: The contents of this class are organized in problem-solving order. Read it slowly.

paragraphs: The first thing to do when your agent responds strangely is to open a trace. A trace is an entire workflow, and the spans within it show the agent execution, LLM creation, tool invocation, and handoff in chronological order. Don't guess, start from the record.

If you find an odd spot in your records, narrow down the cause by component. If the wrong agent responded, check the description of the handover target and handoff span. If the tool was called with an incorrect value, check the tool schema and docstring. If the response continues endlessly, check max_turns. If you don't remember the conversation, look at your session settings.

If you use the Agents API, first determine which unit the failure occurred in. Request errors are read as HTTP status and error objects, turn and session failures are read as post-event queries, and environment failures are read as environment.error. Temporary errors are retried a limited number of times.

When making a new connection, the tool only connects to trusted servers with minimal privileges and requires approval for sensitive operations. If the organizational policy is to not allow tracing, the log must be designed in a different way. In this case, the app compensates by directly logging input and output.
By writing this sequence down in your team's operating documents, you can ensure everyone has the same starting point if a problem arises.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The parts may seem like a lot, but the question is simple. Is it a problem of definition, a problem of loops, a problem of tools, or a problem of memory? Traces are the quickest clue to these four.

If max_turns is exceeded, a MaxTurnsExceeded exception is raised.
Group traces of the same conversation by group_id
Turn off tracing to prevent repeated calls from being recorded

glossary.def: An executor that takes agents and input and runs LLM calls, tools, and handoff loops.
It seems like a tool to LLM, a device for handing over work to other agents.
This is a check that verifies input and output in parallel with the agent and fails quickly if it does not pass.
It is a structure that records an entire workflow and individual tasks within it in chronological order.
A control plane that runs model and tool loops and maintains sessions.
This is a way to call another agent like a tool. The calling agent retains control and the final answer; handoff transfers control.

misconceptions.myth: Handoff is a special control flow.
misconceptions.fact: To LLM, this appears to be a tool call starting with transfer_to_, which causes the Runner to switch the current agent and loop again.

misconceptions.myth: The MCP server is safe as long as you connect.
misconceptions.fact: The MCP server exposes data in the model context and operates in its own capacity, and the model can follow the instructions in the content returned by the server. Only connect to trusted servers with minimal privileges and require approval for sensitive operations.

misconceptions.myth: Tracing can always be turned on.
misconceptions.fact: Tracing is not available in organizations with a zero data retention policy, and can be turned off on a per-run basis.

closing.lead: The key contents of this class are summarized as follows.
points: The Agent is an LLM with instructions, tools, and handoffs, and the Runner loops it.
The loop repeats tool calls and handoffs until the final output is produced, with max_turns preventing congestion.
Tools are divided into hosted, local, function, and agent-as-tools, and MCP servers only connect to trusted ones with minimal privileges.
Sessions connect conversation records, and tracing shows what happened with traces and spans.
The Agents API reads errors by request, turn, session, and environment.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for you to think about for yourself. We will not submit or grade your answers, so feel free to think about them.
closing.reflection: When my agent responds strangely, which parts (definition, loop, tool, session, trace) would I check first?

title: The components of the OpenAI Agents SDK
